spec_choices.why: The designer fixed the table at 4. The auctioneer rotation, the tie-break order and the card counts (4 auctions per player plus 1 unused card each, with 4 cards set aside) all depend on exactly 4 seats.

spec_choices.what: Talk kept as a simultaneous poll each auction, broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The rules specify it. Players have opposing interests (an auctioneer wants high bids, a bidder wants a cheap buy, and nominations push artists up or down), so non-binding talk gives them something to bluff and reason about.

spec_choices.what: Ranking and the bid tie-break are computed as numeric keys
spec_choices.why: This puts the stated tie-break orders into plain arithmetic without changing them.

spec_choices.what: The ranking expression adds 1 to money and requires a value of at least 1
spec_choices.why: An eligible player with 0 money still beats every ineligible player, and if nobody is eligible nobody wins.
Players balance spending against later payouts, use nominations to steer which artists place, read whose talk is a bluff, and make sure they buy 3 paintings to stay eligible.

simplifications.what: The source's 'draw' among eligible players tied for most money becomes a shared win
simplifications.why: The engine has no separate draw; players level at the top share the win, which is the equivalent outcome. 'No eligible player' becomes no winner through min_to_win.

simplifications.what: Each auction is one round; the season-end steps carry a when-condition (auction_in_season == 4)
simplifications.why: The step list is flat, so each season-end step is a single conditional step rather than a separate block.

variation.original_summary: Modern Art is a 3-5 player auction game. Players take turns selling painting cards from five artists under several auction formats. Artists that are played most often in a round pay their owners values that build up over four rounds, and the player with the most money at the end wins.

review.evidence: Never bidding leaves you with only auctioneer income. Overbidding loses money. Prices depend on rankings that the players themselves shape. In the original, seat order matters a little, because the round-ending player gets a timing edge. In the previously tested 12-auction variation seat order mattered a lot: seats 3 and 4 had about 7.5 more expected auctioneer income in the high-value season, and seat 4 alone chose the final Season 2 ranking with full information.
The deal decides which artists you can push, but valuation, timing of the round-ending card, and pricing your own auctions dominate. Experienced players reliably beat novices.
Valuing a painting needs a forecast of the rankings, of opponents' hands and of their incentives. There is no closed-form solution. A weak player still earns from selling cards.

Hands are hidden and future rankings are uncertain. You must infer which artists rivals hold and will push, and plan across rounds because values accumulate. In the previous variation, money was claimed as hidden but was fully computable from announced prices.

Rankings, values, payouts and the winner are pure arithmetic. The previous variation's bid tie-break said 'clockwise from the auctioneer's left' without defining the direction in seat numbers, so the same tie could be resolved differently.

Open ascending and once-around auctions need long sequential bidding chains. Five auction types and five artists push the step and attribute budgets. A round of variable length that ends on the fifth card is awkward. The sealed-bid core fits well.

problems: P1: Open, once-around, fixed-price and double auctions need many sequential steps and conditional blocks, which the engine cannot branch between.
P2: Seat asymmetry in the previous variation. Some seats auctioned twice in the low-value season and others twice in the high-value season, an edge of about 7.5 money.

P3: Full-information kingmaker. The auctioneer of a season's last card alone fixes that season's ranking before bidding. A simple rotation cannot remove this edge, because seasons differ in value and the seat holding the final card of the richest season gains most.
P4: The bid tie-break was undefined: 'clockwise' and 'left' were never mapped to seat numbers.
P5: Money was claimed as hidden but was computable from announced prices, so the claimed hidden element was false.
P6: Fixed artist tie priority (Red > Blue > Green > Yellow) in every season permanently favours holders of Red.

changes.what: Use one auction type only: a simultaneous sealed first-price bid in which every player, including the auctioneer, bids.
changes.why: One poll per auction fits the engine and keeps valuation as the core skill.

changes.what: Use 16 auctions in 4 seasons of 4. The auctioneer order rotates each season: S1 seats 1,2,3,4; S2 seats 2,3,4,1; S3 seats 3,4,1,2; S4 seats 4,1,2,3. Deal 5 cards each from 24, leaving each player one spare card.
changes.why: Every seat auctions exactly once in every value tier, so expected auctioneer income is equal.

changes.what: Add a season-end nomination. After the 4th auction of a season, every player secretly and simultaneously names one artist, and each nomination adds 1 to that artist's season count before ranking. The 4 nominations weigh as much as the 4 cards played that season.
changes.why: The last card no longer settles the ranking. The last painting is bought without knowing the final ranking. The power to decide the ranking is shared by all four players at once, so they must predict each other's nominations.

changes.what: Make the bid tie-break explicit. Tied highest bidders are ordered auctioneer+1, auctioneer+2, auctioneer+3 (seat numbers, with 5 wrapping to 1, 6 to 2, 7 to 3), with the auctioneer last.
changes.why: This gives an arithmetic, unambiguous result. It rotates with the auctioneer, so it is symmetric over a season.

changes.what: After each sale, announce only the artist and the buyer. The price is told privately to the buyer and the auctioneer only.
changes.why: Money becomes genuinely hidden, so players must infer rivals' wealth and standing from their behaviour and their talk.

changes.what: Break artist ranking ties by higher cumulative value, then by a priority that rotates each season (S1 R>B>G>Y, S2 B>G>Y>R, S3 G>Y>R>B, S4 Y>R>B>G).
changes.why: No artist is favoured over the whole game, and established artists keep a natural edge.

changes.what: Starting money becomes 100, and a player must buy at least 3 paintings to be eligible to win.
changes.why: Players can afford Season 3-4 prices, and the 'never buy' policy stays losing over 16 auctions.

keeps: Players auction paintings from their own hands, and the auctioneer profits from others' purchases.
Artist popularity is set by how often an artist appears in a season. Only the top three pay out.
Values accumulate over seasons, so a repeatedly popular artist becomes very valuable.
Paintings are discarded after each season payout.
The winner is the player with the most money, decided by arithmetic.

recommendation.reason: The sealed-bid core with rotating auctioneers fits the engine. A shared simultaneous nomination removes the single-seat kingmaker without changing the game's identity.

variation.name: Modern Art: Four Seasons
variation.summary: Four players auction paintings from four artists in 16 sealed-bid auctions over 4 seasons. Auctioneer duty rotates evenly. At each season's end every player secretly nominates an artist to boost. Artist values accumulate, prices are private, and the richest eligible player wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP.
- Four players sit in seats 1-4.
- The deck has 24 cards: 6 each of Red, Blue, Green and Yellow.
- Shuffle the deck and deal each player 5 cards as a hidden hand. The remaining 4 cards are set aside unseen.
- Each player starts with 100 money. Money is hidden; each player sees only their own.
- Every artist starts with cumulative value 0 and season count 0.

STRUCTURE.
- There are 16 auctions in 4 seasons. Season s contains auctions 4s-3 to 4s.
- In auction k of season s, where k is 1 to 4 within the season, the auctioneer is seat ((s + k - 2) mod 4) + 1.
- This gives the order: Season 1: 1,2,3,4. Season 2: 2,3,4,1. Season 3: 3,4,1,2. Season 4: 4,1,2,3.
- Each player is auctioneer exactly once per season (4 times in all) and ends with 1 unused card.

EACH AUCTION.
(1) The auctioneer privately chooses one card from their hand and removes it from the hand. Its artist is announced to all.
(2) That artist's season count rises by 1, whether or not the painting sells.
(3) Talk: every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others' messages. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages are not binding.
(4) Every player, including the auctioneer, submits a sealed bid at the same time. A bid is a whole number from 0 to the bidder's current money.
(5) Resolution.
  - If the highest bid is 0, the painting is unsold and discarded.
  - Otherwise the highest bidder buys it. If several players tie for highest, the buyer is the first of them in the order: seat (A mod 4)+1, seat ((A+1) mod 4)+1, seat ((A+2) mod 4)+1, then the auctioneer, where A is the auctioneer's seat.
  - The buyer pays the bid. If the buyer is not the auctioneer, the auctioneer receives the bid divided by 2, rounded down, and the rest goes to the bank. If the auctioneer buys, the whole bid goes to the bank.
  - The painting joins the buyer's collection, and the buyer's paintings-bought count rises by 1.
(6) Announcement.
  - Everyone is told the artist and the buyer, or that the painting went unsold.
  - The price is told privately to the buyer and to the auctioneer only.
  - Losing bids are never revealed.

SEASON END (after the 4th auction of each season).
(a) Nomination. Every player at the same time secretly names one of the four artists. Each nomination adds 1 to that artist's season count. All nominations are then revealed.
(b) Ranking. Rank the artists by season count, higher first. Break ties first by higher cumulative value, then by this season's priority: Season 1 R>B>G>Y; Season 2 B>G>Y>R; Season 3 G>Y>R>B; Season 4 Y>R>B>G. An artist with season count 0 cannot place.
(c) Values. Add 30 to the cumulative value of the 1st artist, 20 to the 2nd and 10 to the 3rd. The 4th artist gains nothing.
(d) Payout. For each painting a player owns of an artist that placed in the top three this season, the bank pays that player the artist's cumulative value (after step c). Paintings of an artist that did not place pay 0. Each player is told their own payout privately. The artists' cumulative values are public.
(e) All owned paintings are discarded, and all season counts reset to 0.

GAME END. The game ends after the Season 4 payout. Final money totals are then revealed.
variation.objective: Only players who bought at least 3 paintings during the game are eligible. Among eligible players, the one with the most money wins. If two or more eligible players tie for most money, the game is a draw. If no player is eligible, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect:
Every seat now holds the same opportunities in every value tier. The season's last card is one count among eight, and the final say is a simultaneous nomination by all four players, so no seat has a kingmaker edge.

Players must value paintings under two kinds of uncertainty:
- which artists rivals still hold, inferred from the cards they have played and from their hands;
- how rivals will nominate, predictable from what each has bought.

Hidden prices make standings uncertain, so late-game bidding requires estimating rivals' money from their behaviour.

Talk passes both tests. Players disagree because the auctioneer wants high prices, bidders want low ones, and owners want different artists promoted. A player who follows a call such as 'let's all nominate Blue' or 'nobody bid above 20' may help the speaker's collection or sale at their own expense. Talk lets players propose nomination alliances, bluff about their hands and test promises over seasons.

Thoughtless policies all lose:
- Bid 0: never eligible, so it loses whenever anyone buys 3 paintings.
- Bid all money: overpays by tens in Season 1 and is then broke.
- Fixed bid: buys only overpriced or undervalued junk, depending on the other bids.
- Always play your first card, or always nominate Red: gives up control of the rankings.

The game is not about cooperation, so a highest-total winner does not cause endgame unraveling.

balanced.evidence:
PAINTING VALUES. In Season 1 a 1st/2nd/3rd/4th artist painting pays 30/20/10/0. In Season 2 it pays the artist's Season 1 value plus 30/20/10, or 0 if the artist is not in this season's top three. So Season 2 paintings run from 0 to 60, roughly double Season 1. The sealed auction is first-price: you pay your bid and buy if highest. No bid is dominant, because bidding below value risks losing the painting and bidding above it loses money.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE.
(a) Always bid 0. You never buy, so you are never eligible. You lose every game in which any opponent buys 2 or more paintings, which is almost all of them.
(b) Always bid all money. You win auction 1 for 60, and no painting can pay more than 30 in Season 1. You lose at least 30 net, and afterwards hold only auctioneer income. You lose against sensible and against random play.
(c) Always bid a fixed amount such as 15. This buys only underpriced paintings when others bid low. Against value bidders it buys rarely or overpays on bottom-ranked artists. It does not guarantee a win.
(d) Always play the first card in hand. This gives up control of the artist rankings. It does not guarantee a win.
No policy wins or draws almost every time, so the winner-rule test is passed.

SEAT ASYMMETRY (the failure). The auctioneer order is:
- Season 1 (auctions 1-6): seats 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2.
- Season 2 (auctions 7-12): seats 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Seats 1 and 2 auction twice in the low-value season. Seats 3 and 4 auction twice in the high-value season. Take rough equilibrium prices near value, about 15 in Season 1 and about 30 in Season 2, with the auctioneer receiving half.

| Seats | Season 1 sales | Season 2 sales | Expected auctioneer income |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 and 2 | 2 x 7.5 | 1 x 15 | about 30 |
| 3 and 4 | 1 x 7.5 | 2 x 15 | about 37.5 |

That is a structural edge of about 7.5 money for seats 3 and 4, in a game where margins are a few tens.

Worse, the card the auctioneer reveals at the last auction of a season fixes that season's final ranking before anyone bids. In Season 2, auction 12 belongs to seat 4. Every collection and every price is public, so seat 4 chooses, with full information, which artist finishes 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th. That swings each owned Season 2 painting by up to 60. Seat 2 holds the same power in Season 1 at smaller stakes. Seat 4 gets both the extra high-value sales and the final kingmaker card.

TIE-BREAK. Ties go to the seats left of the auctioneer first, so seats are not symmetric within an auction either. This is minor next to the above.

Both players realistically can win, but the seat order gives seat 4 a clear, systematic edge.

SIDE NOTE. 'Hidden money' is not really hidden. Every winning price is announced and the auctioneer's half is deterministic, so all money totals can be computed from public information. The design claims this as a hidden element.

playable.evidence:
Card accounting checks out. 12 auctions with each player auctioneer 3 times uses 3 of 4 cards; 16 cards are dealt and 8 set aside. Budgets are within limits: steps 15 of 20, choices 3 (card, message, bid) of 4, attributes 18 of 20, hidden elements 2 of 3, random draws 0, rounds 12 of 40. Season end can run as `when`-conditioned steps after auctions 6 and 12. The ranking with fixed tie-priority uses the arithmetic_ranking workaround with calc, which is supported. The game is finite and decided by money arithmetic. Bids are simultaneous polls.

Talk is appropriate. The four players disagree:
- the auctioneer wants a high price;
- bidders want a low one;
- owners want different artists promoted.
So talk can mislead or coordinate, and following a proposal can cost you. Talk is simultaneous, as required.

The defect is an undefined tie-break. Rule (5) says ties go to 'the tied bidder who comes first clockwise starting from the seat to the auctioneer's left'. The rules never say whether clockwise or 'left' means increasing or decreasing seat number. The auction rotation 1, 2, 3, 4 is called 'rotation', not clockwise. Two models or the engine could resolve the same tie differently. Ties are likely here: bids are integers, and the painting's value is fully known at season-final auctions. This rule decides who buys, so it must be arithmetic and explicit.

required_changes: Remove the seat asymmetry. Use 16 auctions in 4 seasons of 4 (cumulative values as in the original). Each seat is auctioneer once per season, with the starting seat rotating: Season 1 seats 1,2,3,4; Season 2 seats 2,3,4,1; Season 3 seats 3,4,1,2; Season 4 seats 4,1,2,3. Every seat then auctions equally often in each value tier and holds the season-final card exactly once. Deal 5 cards each (20 of 24, 4 set aside) so each player has one spare card. Rounds become 16, within the 40 limit.

Alternatively, keep 12 auctions but make the season-final card not count toward the ranking, or fix the ranking before the last auction of each season. Then the last auctioneer is not a full-information kingmaker. Also give each seat the same number of Season 2 auctions.
Replace the tie-break wording with an explicit seat order: ties go to seat (auctioneer mod 4)+1, then the next seat in increasing number wrapping 4 to 1, with the auctioneer last.

Either drop the claim that money is hidden, or make some transfer genuinely private (for example, announce only the artist and buyer, not the price). The hidden_elements count should then reflect what is actually hidden.

balanced.evidence:
PAINTING VALUE TABLE. A placed painting pays its artist's cumulative value after the season's increment. An artist can gain at most 30 per season. Upper bounds per painting: S1 30/20/10 for 1st/2nd/3rd; S2 up to 60; S3 up to 90; S4 up to 120. An unplaced artist pays 0.

MAIN DECISION (sealed first-price bid b on a painting worth V to you):
- If you win and you are not the auctioneer: you net V-b, the auctioneer nets floor(b/2), the other two net 0.
- In a 4-player most-money race, buying beats letting the auctioneer profit only when V-b > b/2, that is b < 2V/3. Example: S1 leader V=30 gives b<20; S4 V=120 gives b<80.
- If the auctioneer buys their own card, they net V-b and nobody else gains. This lets an auctioneer cap a price, but they pay the full b to the bank.
- So there is a real valuation-and-shading trade-off. No bid level is strictly best regardless of the others.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE:
(1) Always bid 0. Never buys, so never eligible (3 paintings needed). Against sensible play it LOSES every game. Against random play it also loses, since random bidders buy plenty. It draws only if nobody reaches 3. Fails as a strategy.
(2) Always bid all money. Wins auction 1 at 100 (tie-break aside), then holds 0 money until a payout of at most 30. It wins later auctions only at tiny or zero bids. It finishes far below a player who bought at sensible prices, so it LOSES against sensible play. Against random play it overpays on every win and usually loses.
(3) Always bid 1. Wins only when every opponent bids 0, i.e. on worthless paintings. Against sensible play it rarely reaches positive value. It can lose eligibility or end with low money. It does not never-lose.
(4) Always nominate the first artist (Red). This is one vote in 8 season counts. Opponents' card choices and nominations override it, so it does not guarantee a win or a draw.
No policy never loses.

SEAT EDGE:
- Auctioneer order rotates (1234, 2341, 3412, 4123). Every seat is first, second, third and last auctioneer once.
- The buy-tie order is relative to the auctioneer, so it also rotates.
- Season tie priorities are public and colour-based, not seat-based.
- Information is symmetric: hidden hand, hidden money, private price.
- No structural seat advantage.

All four players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS.
- Every phase is specified: card choice, count increment, simultaneous talk, sealed bid bounded by current money, sale or no sale at a top bid of 0, a deterministic tie order relative to auctioneer seat A, payment split with floor, and what is announced to whom.
- Season end is specified: simultaneous nomination, ranking by count, then cumulative value, then a per-season colour priority. This is a total order.
- The rule that a count-0 artist cannot place is clear. With 8 counts per season (4 auctions + 4 nominations), at most 3 artists can be left unplaced. If fewer than 3 artists have counts, the lower prizes are simply not awarded. This is implied but readable.
- Hand arithmetic holds: 4 players x 5 cards = 20 dealt, 4 set aside, 16 auctioned, 1 card left per player.

FINITE AND ARITHMETIC. The game has a fixed 16 auctions. The winner is decided by an eligibility count (≥3) plus the highest money, with ties drawn. All numbers are kept by the game.

LIMITS. Stated 15 steps/round ≤20.
- Choice steps: auctioneer card, talk, bid, plus the nomination in season-end rounds. That makes 4 at most, within the limit of 4.
- Attributes 18 ≤20. Hidden elements 2 ≤3 (hands, money; prices are private messages).
- Random draws 0 per round; the shuffle happens once at setup. Rounds 16 ≤40.

ENGINE FIT.
- Season-end steps run as single steps with a `when` condition (auction number mod 4 = 0). This is a per-step condition, not a block choice, so it is allowed.
- Ranking 4 artists with tie-breaks needs calc (the arithmetic_ranking workaround). That is feasible inside the step budget.
- No board, clock, trade or binding agreement is needed.
- All simultaneous choices (talk, bid, nomination) are polls.

TALK. With 4 players there is real disagreement, because players own different artists and want different ones to place. Following another player's proposal ('everyone nominate Blue', 'don't bid on Green') can cost you. It also gives material to reason about: bluffing about hands and holdings. Talk is simultaneous, as required.

ENDGAME. This is not a cooperate/betray matrix. Late rounds still require valuing paintings and steering nominations, and there is no safe option that wins every late round. Bidding 0 risks ineligibility and forgoes S4 values of up to 120.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHERE CHANCE ENTERS. The only randomness is the initial 5-card deal from 6 of each of 4 colours, plus 4 hidden cards.
- A skewed hand (e.g. 3 of one colour) gives some influence over season counts.
- But each player plays only 1 card per season. Nominations add as many counts as auctions do.
- Every painting is open to every bidder.
- I estimate the deal accounts for roughly 15-25% of outcome variance.

WHAT GOOD PLAY CONTROLS:
- Valuing paintings: the expected rank of each artist given announced counts and inferred hands.
- Bid shading against hidden money. Rivals' money can be partly reconstructed from buys and payouts, but not from exact prices.
- Choosing which card to auction, and when.
- Coalition-building through nominations and talk.
- Meeting the 3-painting eligibility cheaply.

INFERENCE TARGETS. There is plenty to infer and act on: opponents' remaining colours, from cards played so far (24 total, 4 unseen); rivals' collections, which are public by buyer announcements and reveal their nomination incentives; and rivals' budgets.

OUTCOME UNDER EQUAL GOOD PLAY. If all four play well, the winner is decided by bid-shading accuracy, nomination coordination and timing, not by the deal alone. A weak deal can be overcome by buying other players' auctioned paintings and joining nomination blocs. A careful reasoner clearly beats a thoughtless one: see the policy analysis under balanced.

triage.reason: The game file works as specified, but the design lets a thoughtless policy dominate. Always taking the first option, in practice bidding 0 and never spending, wins about 98% of decided matches. Always taking the last option, bidding everything, loses about 90%. Holding cash beats competing for paintings, which is a flaw in the economy, not in the code.
triage.guidance:
Rebalance the auction so that never buying is not a winning default and overbidding is not the only way to lose.
1) Make paintings reliably worth buying. Season payouts are small next to 100 starting money: in season 1 only the top two artists pay, at 30 and 20 per painting. Raise first_artist_gain and second_artist_gain, or lower starting_money, so a painting bought at a fair price is a clear profit.
2) Penalise sitting out. For example, make the winner's score money plus the current value of paintings held. Or charge every player a small upkeep each season. Or have the auctioneer pay the bank when the card goes unsold or free, so a passive player bleeds money.
3) Narrow the bid options so a single extreme is less degenerate. Replace 0-to-all-money with a few levels tied to the artist's current value (for example 0, 10, 20, 30, 40), so a random or maximal bid cannot throw away the whole bankroll in one auction.
4) Re-check seat balance after the change. Seats 1 and 2 also auctioneer first and collect sale proceeds.
Aim for no fixed first-option or last-option policy to win much more than its fair share against random seats.

triage.guidance:
Rebalance so that refusing to bid is not a safe win. Options:
(1) Raise painting values relative to starting money, e.g. 100/70/40 with less starting money, so buying at a fair price is clearly profitable.
(2) Make hoarding cash cost something, e.g. money counts at half value at game end, or the player with the fewest paintings loses a penalty.
(3) Make it harder for an auctioneer to profit when everyone else passes, e.g. an unsold painting goes to the auctioneer only if they paid a reserve to the bank.
(4) Pay part of each winning bid to the bank rather than to the auctioneer, so passivity is not subsidised.
Keep the rules arithmetic and simultaneous. Then re-check that neither always-min nor always-max bidding beats random seats by a wide margin.
